In Africa, the U.S. is cutting trade benefits for some partners while signing major investment agreements with others. After moving to end South Africa’s duty-free access to the U.S. market, Washington has recently signed a five-year economic agreement with Egypt worth $625 million.
Picture collage President Vladimir Putin of Russia, United States President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping. [Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP/Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images; Ng Han Guan/Pool/Getty Images; Time] The U.S. is adjusting its economic ties in Africa by cutting trade benefits for some countries like South Africa while boosting investment in others such as Egypt. South Africa will lose its duty-free access to the U.S. market under AGOA from 2027 due to policy concerns, which may lead to higher tariffs on its exports. In contrast, the U.S. has signed a five-year, $625 million economic agreement with Egypt, covering sectors like energy, agriculture, and artificial intelligence. This shift comes as the U.S. faces growing competition from China and Russia, both of which are increasing their economic presence in Africa. The U.S. government announced plans to end South Africa’s duty-free access under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) from January 1, 2027.
South Africa is the programme’s largest beneficiary. In 2025, it exported about $1.7 billion worth of goods to the U.S. without paying import duties. These products included vehicles, textiles and agricultural goods.
South African citrus growers say orchards planted for the US market cannot be redirected quickly to countries with different import rules and consumer preferences. [AgriNews.co.za] BI Africa U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated, “ President Trump found that the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA's eligibility criteria ”.
South Africa has said it wants to resolve the dispute before the planned cutoff date.
U.S. representatives have also indicated that trade between the two countries will continue.
However, South African products that lose AGOA benefits could face higher import duties in the American market .
While moving to tighten trade rules for South Africa, Washington has signed a five-year, $625 million framework agreement with Egypt to support economic growth in both countries.
Egyptian foreign affairs officials and U.S. Chargé d'Affaires Robert Silverman witnessed the signing.
Egypt and the United States have formalized a new five-year Agreement valued at $625 million [Image Credit: Egypt Today] Google The agreement covers several areas, including water management, clean energy, healthcare, artificial intelligence and agriculture.
It is expected to support projects that use American technology and create more business opportunities between the two countries.
The deal comes as the U.S. seeks to strengthen its economic ties across Africa while China and Russia expand their presence on the continent. Both countries have built relationships through investment, financing and other economic partnerships, adding to competition for influence in the region.
Through agreements such as the one with Egypt, Washington is seeking to expand opportunities for American businesses and strengthen its economic relationships with key African partners.
Unlike the Alliance of Sahel States, which has rejected Western influence and embraced Russia, Egypt has chosen a multilateral relationship with the world's most powerful countries.
Russia agrees to build nuclear power plant for Burkina Faso [Africa Briefing] Pulse Nigeria Recently, Egypt concluded its "Eagles of Civilization 2026" joint air exercise with China.
Meanwhile, Russia has expanded its economic influence by funding 85% of Egypt's El Dabaa nuclear power plant through long-term state loans.
Despite these growing Eastern ties, Cairo continues to maintain a cordial strategic relationship with Washington.
Reports from Business Insider Africa note that the United States recently waived human rights conditions attached to $320 million in military aid to Egypt, facilitating the release of these funds as Washington moves to strengthen its security partnership with Cairo amid escalating conflict with Iran.
This pragmatic release of funding aligns directly with broader U.S. foreign policy ; as documented in African Perspectives Journal published by Egypt's State Information Service, " US funding will be directed to key countries and key strategic objectives, and that all US aid on the continent will advance US interests".
Together, these financial and diplomatic actions demonstrate how Washington leverages foreign aid and security assistance as targeted tools to solidify alliances, secure critical regional hubs, and project greater global influence over rival powers.
Egypt's balancing of influence, however, has sparked greater competition among global powers, with each nation seeking to exert greater influence through defense pacts, investments, project execution, and funding.
Consequently, every move made by a world power to strengthen its influence serves as an indirect attempt to weaken the leverage of its global competitors
